questions.q: Pramod runs a banana farm in Jalgaon and wants thousands of healthy plantlets from one high-yielding plant, with virus-infected plants eliminated. Which method should he choose?
questions.a: Tissue culture, growing plantlets from the shoot tip of the plant
o: Tissue culture, growing plantlets from the shoot tip of the plant
Layering, burying the middle of a low branch in soil until roots grow
Grafting, fitting a stem piece of a good variety into a slit of a rooted plant
Planting seeds from its fruits, which would make the plantlets differ from each other

questions.q: Meena keeps two identical boxes of moist roti, one in a 30 degree Celsius cupboard and the other in a refrigerator. Fuzzy patches appear only in the cupboard box on day 3. What best explains this?
questions.a: Mould spores need warmth and moisture, and low temperatures slow or stop their reproduction
o: Mould spores need warmth and moisture, and low temperatures slow or stop their reproduction
Refrigeration destroys every spore on the roti, so mould cannot grow on it even later
Mould forms only on warm roti because the roti itself slowly produces the fungus
Cold air carries away all the water, so spores in the fridge could not have been present

questions.q: A hydra in a school aquarium shows three outgrowths of different sizes on its body at the same time. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Each outgrowth formed by repeated cell division at one site and will separate when it has enlarged
o: Each outgrowth formed by repeated cell division at one site and will separate when it has enlarged
The outgrowths are spores that will float away on air currents and germinate on moist surfaces
The outgrowths are eggs that formed when sperm from another hydra fused with the parent
Only the largest outgrowth is a bud, while the smaller ones are separate small organisms attached to it

questions.q: A moist roti left in a closed dabba grows fuzzy patches in three days. Rahul says, 'The roti must have made the mould by itself, because there was none when it was fresh.' Which reply fits what the chapter says about Louis Pasteur's work?
questions.a: New life always comes from pre-existing life, so the mould grew from spores already in the air
o: New life always comes from pre-existing life, so the mould grew from spores already in the air
He is right, because living things can arise by themselves from non-living matter such as moist food
He is right, because mould appears only when the food has already rotted from the inside
He is wrong, because the mould must have grown from the dabba itself and not from the air

questions.q:
Statement 1: Every Bryophyllum plantlet that sprouts on a leaf is genetically identical to the parent plant.
Statement 2: Spores of Rhizopus form after the fusion of two gametes from different mould colonies.
Statement 3: In grafting, a stem piece of Plant B is fitted into a slit made on a rooted Plant A.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Plantlets sprouting from one Bryophyllum leaf are clones of the parent plant.
Reason (R): The plantlets arise by mitosis, which gives daughter cells with the same number of identical chromosomes as the parent cell.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A yeast culture starts with one cell, and every cell produces one bud that grows into a new cell each hour. After 4 hours the culture has ___ cells, all clones of the first cell.

Match the vegetative propagation method with what is done.
1. Cutting
2. Grafting
3. Layering
4. Tissue culture
a. Plantlets mass-produced from a shoot tip, helping to eliminate virus-infected plants
b. A stem piece of one variety fitted into a slit of a rooted plant of another variety
c. The middle of a flexible twig is buried in soil and cut from the parent once roots form
d. Shoot pieces with lower leaves removed are planted at 45 to 60 degrees in compost-mixed soil

A farmer owns one mother banana plant that gives a heavy yield.
(a) Name the lab technique that gives thousands of virus-free plantlets and the plant part used to make them.
(b) Why will these plantlets also carry the mother plant's high-yield trait?
questions.a: (a) Tissue culture, using the shoot tip (apical meristem). (b) They come from one parent by mitosis, so they are genetically identical clones.
s: Part (a): tissue culture from the shoot tip (apical meristem)
Part (b): one parent and mitosis give genetically identical individuals

questions.q: True or False? Because mould spores are lightweight and single-celled, a mould colony on bread can spread only if a hand touches the bread. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Spores float easily through air currents and settle on moist food, so no touch is needed.
s: Verdict: False
Reason or correction: Spores float easily through air currents and settle on moist food, so no touch is needed

questions.q:
Ginger sprouts new plants from its fleshy underground stem, while Bryophyllum sprouts plantlets on its leaves.
(a) Name the part of the parent from which the new plant arises in each.
(b) State what the two cases have in common that makes both vegetative propagation.
questions.a: (a) Ginger: the fleshy underground stem; Bryophyllum: the leaf. (b) In both, a vegetative (growing) part of one parent gives rise to a new plant, so the offspring are genetically identical.
s: Part (a): underground stem for ginger, leaf for Bryophyllum
Part (b): a growing part of a single parent forms a new plant without seeds, giving identical offspring

questions.q:
A gardener at a nursery wants a yellow rose flowering on a hardy wild rose root.
(a) Which vegetative propagation method suits this?
(b) Why is the cut or slit wrapped with cloth or film until it heals?
questions.a: (a) Grafting, fitting a yellow rose stem piece into a slit of a rooted wild rose. (b) To keep pests from entering the wound until the graft heals.
s: Part (a): grafting of the stem piece onto the rooted plant
Part (b): wrapping protects the wound from pests until it heals

questions.q: Two sealed boxes of the same bread are moistened equally. One is kept at 30 degrees Celsius and the other at 8 degrees Celsius. Which box will show mould sooner, and what does the mould grow from?
questions.a: The 30 degree box, because spores need warmth to grow and lower temperatures slow or stop their reproduction; the mould grows from spores that were already present on the bread or in the air.
s: The warmer box shows mould first because lower temperatures slow or stop spore reproduction
The mould grows from spores already present, not from the bread itself

questions.q: Anita says, 'Every organism that reproduces asexually does so by releasing spores, because with only one parent there is nothing else it can do.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. Spore formation is one method; asexual reproduction also occurs by vegetative propagation in plants (potato, Bryophyllum) and by budding (yeast, hydra).
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Counter-example: budding in hydra or yeast
Second counter-example: vegetative propagation in plants such as potato or Bryophyllum

questions.q: Write a situation in which a person grows ten new plants from one parent plant without using any seeds. Name the method, say which part is used, and explain why the ten plants are alike.
questions.a: E.g. a farmer cuts a sugarcane stem into ten pieces and plants them: the method is cutting, the stem is used, and all ten are clones because they come from one parent by mitosis.
s: A realistic situation with the part used
Correct method named for that situation
Identical offspring explained by one parent and mitosis

questions.q: A grower plants 500 banana plants, all produced by tissue culture from one mother plant. Using what the chapter says about how such plants arise, state what is true about their genetic make-up and predict one risk of planting only such plants.
questions.a: They are genetically identical clones from mitosis of one parent. A risk: since they are all alike, a problem that harms one plant can harm every plant in the orchard.
s: Plants are genetically identical clones from one parent
Reason: mitosis gives daughter cells identical to the parent cell
A reasoned risk of no variation among the plants

questions.q:
A yeast culture starts with 1 cell. Every cell grows one bud each hour and the bud becomes a new cell. Assume no cell dies.
(i) How many cells are there after 6 hours?
(ii) How many after 10 hours?
(iii) After how many whole hours does the culture first exceed 1000 cells?
(iv) How many of the cells are genetically identical to the first cell?
(v) Name the cell division that makes this possible and say what it does to chromosome number.
questions.a: (i) 64 (ii) 1024 (iii) 10 hours (iv) all of them (v) Mitosis; each daughter cell has the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell.
s: After 6 hours: 2 to the power 6 = 64 cells
After 10 hours: 2 to the power 10 = 1024 cells
1000 is first exceeded at 10 hours, since 512 is below 1000
All cells are clones, being formed from one parent without gametes
Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same as in the parent cell

questions.q:
A horticulture trainer gives four tasks. Choose the best vegetative propagation method for each and justify with one feature of the method.
(i) Planting 2 acres with sugarcane using pieces of its stem.
(ii) Starting a new lemon plant from a flexible twig while it is still attached to the tree.
(iii) Putting two rose varieties on one rooted plant.
(iv) Producing virus-free banana plantlets in large numbers.
(v) Say what all four methods share about the offspring.
questions.a: (i) Cutting: stem pieces grow into new plants. (ii) Layering: the middle of the twig is buried and roots form in 10 to 15 days before it is cut from the tree. (iii) Grafting: a stem piece fitted into a slit of the rooted plant. (iv) Tissue culture from shoot tips. (v) The offspring are genetically identical to the single parent.
s: (i) cutting, justified by stem pieces rooting into new plants
(ii) layering, justified by roots forming on the buried twig before it is cut free
(iii) grafting, justified by the stem piece joining the rooted plant
(iv) tissue culture, justified by mass production from shoot tips
(v) one parent, so identical offspring

questions.q:
Pramod's banana farm in Jalgaon has room for 5000 plants. If he plants offshoots taken from his existing plants, 18 percent turn out virus-infected and give no fruit, and the offshoots cost nothing. If he buys laboratory plantlets at Rs 16 each, only 3 percent are infected. Every healthy plant gives a bunch worth Rs 260 after all other costs.
(a) Name the laboratory technique and the plant part from which such plantlets are grown.
(b) How many healthy plants does he get with offshoots and with laboratory plantlets?
(c) Find his net money for each choice after paying for plantlets.
(d) Should he switch? Give one reason from the numbers and one from how the plantlets are made.
questions.a: (a) Tissue culture; shoot tip (apical meristem). (b) 4100 with offshoots, 4850 with plantlets. (c) Rs 10,66,000 and Rs 11,81,000. (d) Yes, he gains Rs 1,15,000; but all the plants are clones, so a new disease could hit them all, and he could keep part of the field in mixed stock.
s: Tissue culture from the shoot tip (apical meristem)
4100 and 4850 healthy plants
Rs 10,66,000 against Rs 11,81,000 after paying Rs 80,000 for plantlets
Decision backed by the Rs 1,15,000 gain and the clone-uniformity risk

questions.q:
In the school lab, three moist chambers hold identical slices of bread. Chamber A is at 30 degrees Celsius and moist, chamber B is at 30 degrees Celsius but dry, and chamber C is moist at 6 degrees Celsius. After three days only one chamber shows fuzzy patches. The canteen next door wastes 25 rolls a day at Rs 6 each at room temperature; a fridge hired for Rs 100 a day would cut this to 2 rolls a day.
(a) Which chamber shows the patches, and which two conditions does it have?
(b) Where did the mould come from?
(c) Chamber C is shifted to 30 degrees Celsius and stays moist. What do you predict, and why?
(d) Compare the daily cost of waste at room temperature with the cost with the fridge and recommend a choice, naming one factor besides money.
questions.a: (a) Chamber A: warmth and moisture. (b) Spores from the air settled on the bread. (c) Mould will appear after some days, because the cold only slowed the spores' reproduction. (d) Room: Rs 150; fridge: Rs 100 + Rs 12 = Rs 112; hire the fridge, saving Rs 38 a day, and food safety or less spoilage by moulds and bacteria is a further factor.
s: Chamber A, with warmth and moisture
Spores already in the air settled on the bread
Mould appears after warming because low temperature only slows reproduction
Rs 150 against Rs 112 and a reasoned recommendation with a non-money factor

questions.q: A species has 12 chromosomes in each body cell. How many chromosomes will one of its sperm cells carry, and how many will the zygote formed from that sperm and an egg carry?
questions.a: 6 in the sperm and 12 in the zygote
o: 6 in the sperm and 12 in the zygote
12 in the sperm and 24 in the zygote
6 in the sperm and 6 in the zygote
12 in the sperm and 12 in the zygote

questions.q: Two sisters born to the same parents are not genetically identical. Which statement gives the best reason according to the chapter?
questions.a: Chromosome pairs separate in meiosis in a random way, so each gamete carries a different mix
o: Chromosome pairs separate in meiosis in a random way, so each gamete carries a different mix
Each parent hands over exactly half of its body cells, chosen differently each time
The zygote of the younger sister copies the parents' chromosomes with more mistakes
Mitosis in the mother's body cells changes her chromosomes before each pregnancy

questions.q: Four pairs of beads, each pair standing for two contrasting characters on a different chromosome, are used in the bead activity. One bead is picked at random from each pair. How many different combinations can be made?

Suppose a species had no meiosis, so each parent passed its full set of 20 chromosomes into the gamete. Every new generation is formed by two such gametes fusing. How many chromosomes would the body cells of the third generation after the 20-chromosome parents contain?

Statement 1: A human sperm cell carries 46 chromosomes, 23 from each parent.
Statement 2: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number of a diploid parent cell to half in the gametes.
Statement 3: Variation among individuals helps some of them adapt better when the environment changes.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statement 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Each human gamete has 23 chromosomes, although human body cells have 23 pairs.
Reason (R): Each of the 23 pairs consists of two chromosomes inherited from the same parent, and meiosis removes one pair at random.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: With five pairs of contrasting characters on five different chromosomes, picking one bead at random from each pair gives ___ possible combinations.

Match the process or activity with what it gives.
1. Mitosis
2. Meiosis
3. Fusion of an egg and a sperm
4. Bead activity with three pairs
a. Gives eight possible combinations of characters
b. Forms a zygote with the full chromosome number again
c. Gives two daughter cells with the parent's chromosome number
d. Gives haploid gametes from a diploid cell

A species has 26 chromosomes in each body cell.
(a) How many pairs of chromosomes does it have, and how many chromosomes are there in one of its gametes?
(b) Say what happens to the members of each pair during meiosis.
questions.a: (a) 13 pairs and 13 chromosomes in a gamete. (b) The two chromosomes of each pair separate, so each gamete gets only one chromosome from every pair.
s: Part (a): 13 pairs, 13 chromosomes per gamete
Part (b): the chromosomes of each pair separate so a gamete gets one from each pair

questions.q: True or False? In humans, sperm formed by meiosis carry 46 chromosomes so that the zygote can have 46. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. A sperm carries 23 chromosomes and an egg carries 23, and their fusion restores 46 in the zygote.
s: Verdict: False
Reason or correction: A sperm carries 23 chromosomes and an egg carries 23, and their fusion restores 46 in the zygote

questions.q:
Two pairs of beads are used in the bead activity, one bead picked from each pair.
(a) How many combinations are possible?
(b) A third pair is added. How many combinations are possible now, and how does this compare with part (a)?
questions.a: (a) 4. (b) 8, which is double the number in part (a).
s: Part (a): 2 x 2 = 4 combinations
Part (b): 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, twice as many as with two pairs

questions.q: Give one example from the chapter of a human variation that can help a person survive, and explain how variation of this kind contributes to the survival of a species.
questions.a: E.g. tolerating low oxygen at high altitude (or digesting milk in adulthood). Some individuals adapt better when the environment changes, and over time this contributes to evolution.
s: A correct example from the chapter
Variation lets some individuals adapt to changing environments, and so the species survives and evolves

questions.q: Both parents contribute chromosomes in sexual reproduction, yet the number does not double every generation. Explain why, in two steps.
questions.a: Each gamete is made by meiosis and carries only half the parent's chromosomes, so when two gametes fuse the zygote gets back the full number.
s: Meiosis halves the chromosome number in the gametes
Fusion of two haploid gametes restores the full number in the zygote

questions.q: Arjun says, 'If a species has just 3 pairs of chromosomes, one pair of parents could in theory produce a child in 8 x 8 = 64 different combinations.' Check his claim using the bead activity.
questions.a: Yes. Each parent can form 8 different combinations of gametes (2 x 2 x 2), and any egg can meet any sperm, giving 8 x 8 = 64.
s: Verdict: the claim is correct
Each parent's gametes give 8 combinations by random picking
Any of 8 eggs with any of 8 sperm gives 64

questions.q: Design a bead activity that gives exactly 16 combinations. State how many pairs of beads you use, what each pair stands for, and how a combination is made.
questions.a: Use four pairs of beads, each pair standing for two contrasting characters on a different chromosome (for example hair colour, hair type, eye colour and height); pick one bead at random from each pair, giving 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16.
s: Four pairs of beads chosen
Each pair stands for two contrasting characters on a different chromosome
One bead picked from each pair gives 2 to the power 4 = 16

questions.q: A student says, 'If all children of a family were genetically identical, nothing would be lost.' Using the chapter, explain what the species would lose when the environment changes.
questions.a: Without variation, no individual would be better placed to adapt, for example to low oxygen at altitude, so the whole group could suffer together, and the species would have less chance to evolve over time.
s: Variation comes from random mixing of chromosomes in meiosis
Some individuals adapt better when the environment changes
Over time this contributes to evolution, which identical children would lack

questions.q:
A species has 6 pairs of chromosomes. One bead of each pair is picked at random to model a gamete.
(i) How many chromosomes are there in a body cell, and how many in a gamete?
(ii) How many different gamete combinations are possible?
(iii) How many different zygote combinations can form from an egg and a sperm?
(iv) How many chromosomes does the zygote have?
(v) Explain why two siblings of this species usually differ.
questions.a: (i) 12 and 6 (ii) 64 (iii) 4096 (iv) 12 (v) Random separation of the pairs gives each gamete a different mix, so siblings receive different combinations.
s: 12 in a body cell and 6 in a gamete
2 to the power 6 = 64 gamete combinations
64 x 64 = 4096 zygote combinations
Zygote gets 6 + 6 = 12 chromosomes
Random mixing in meiosis gives different combinations to siblings

questions.q: Compare mitosis and meiosis under these heads: (i) the kind of cell that divides and what the daughter cells are, (ii) the chromosome number of the daughter cells compared with the parent cell, (iii) the genetic result, (iv) the type of reproduction each supports, (v) give the human chromosome numbers that show the difference.
questions.a: (i) Mitosis: body or single cells giving daughter cells; meiosis: a diploid parent cell giving gametes. (ii) Mitosis keeps the same number; meiosis halves it. (iii) Mitosis gives identical clones; meiosis gives varied combinations. (iv) Mitosis supports asexual reproduction; meiosis supports sexual reproduction. (v) 46 to 46 in mitosis, 46 to 23 in meiosis.
s: Cells dividing and products
Same chromosome number in mitosis, half in meiosis
Clones from mitosis, variation from meiosis
Asexual against sexual reproduction
46 to 46 and 46 to 23

questions.q:
A school science club of 40 students runs the bead activity with 4 pairs of beads, each student picking one bead from each pair at random and writing the combination. The teacher then says that with all 23 pairs of human chromosomes the picking would be the same, only longer.
(a) How many different combinations are possible with the 4 pairs?
(b) Can all 40 students end up with different combinations? Explain.
(c) How many combinations are possible with 23 pairs, and is this enough for a school of 1200 students to all differ?
(d) The teacher has one class period. Argue for using 4 pairs or all 23 pairs for explaining why siblings differ, using the numbers.
questions.a: (a) 16. (b) No, only 16 combinations exist for 40 students, so some must repeat. (c) 83,88,608, far more than 1200. (d) 4 pairs is quick and shows repeats clearly; 23 pairs is realistic and shows that siblings rarely match, but cannot be done by hand; a mixed approach with 4 pairs then a calculation for 23 pairs works.
s: 2 to the power 4 = 16 combinations
16 is fewer than 40, so repeats are certain
2 to the power 23 = 83,88,608, which is more than 1200
A reasoned choice between the hands-on 4 pairs and the realistic 23 pairs

questions.q:
In a thought experiment, a species X has 10 chromosomes in the body cells of the first generation, and its meiosis fails, so each parent passes on the full set in its gamete. Two such gametes fuse to form each next generation.
(a) How many chromosomes will the body cells have in generations 2, 3 and 4?
(b) In which generation does the number first pass 100?
(c) In real humans with 46 chromosomes, how many would the body cells have two generations later if meiosis failed in the same way?
(d) A student argues, 'More chromosomes means more characters, so failed meiosis would be an advantage.' Judge this using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 20, 40, 80. (b) Generation 5, with 160. (c) 184. (d) The argument fails: the number would keep doubling and the cells could not cope, while the variation that helps survival comes from the random mixing of chromosomes in meiosis, not from extra chromosomes.
s: 160 in generation 5
Judgement based on endless doubling and the role of random mixing for variation

questions.q: A botanist studies a meadow flower with dull petals, no scent or nectar, very light small pollen grains released in huge numbers, and a long feathery stigma. Which pollinator is it most likely adapted to?
questions.a: Wind, as in wheat, maize and rice
o: Wind, as in wheat, maize and rice
Bees and butterflies, as in sunflower and marigold
Water currents, as in Vallisneria and Hydrilla
Sunbirds, as in the coral tree and hibiscus

questions.q: In a pea-plant experiment, every treatment formed fruit except the flower bud whose stamens were removed and which was then wrapped in muslin. Which conclusion does this one result support best?
questions.a: Without pollen reaching the stigma, the flower does not form fruit
o: Without pollen reaching the stigma, the flower does not form fruit
Wrapping a flower in muslin cloth always prevents any fruit from forming
Only flowers that are already fully open can ever go on to form a fruit
Stamens swell and turn into the fruit once the petals have fallen off

questions.q: Pollen lands on the stigma of a hibiscus flower and starts growing a pollen tube. Which description tells where the tube goes and what happens at its end?
questions.a: It grows down the style to the ovary, where the male gamete fuses with an egg cell in an ovule
o: It grows down the style to the ovary, where the male gamete fuses with an egg cell in an ovule
It grows down the filament to the anther, where the male gamete fuses with another pollen grain
It grows through the sepal into the petals, where an embryo forms from the fused cells
It grows over the surface of the stigma only, where the pollen grain splits into an egg and a seed

questions.q: A grass plant releases 6,00,000 pollen grains per flower and forms 120 seeds. An insect-pollinated herb releases 24,000 pollen grains per flower and forms 800 seeds. Which statement fits the numbers?
questions.a: The herb needs far fewer pollen grains per seed, yet the grass can still succeed by releasing huge numbers
o: The herb needs far fewer pollen grains per seed, yet the grass can still succeed by releasing huge numbers
The grass is more efficient because it releases more pollen grains and therefore forms more seeds per flower than the herb does
The herb must be wind-pollinated, since only wind pollination lets so few pollen grains form so many seeds
The two plants need about the same number of pollen grains for each seed that they form

questions.q:
Statement 1: The anther produces pollen grains that contain male gametes.
Statement 2: Insect-pollinated flowers often have a sticky stigma to receive the large, sticky or spiny pollen.
Statement 3: After fertilisation the ovule becomes the fruit and the ovary becomes the seed.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statement 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Wind-pollinated grasses release far more pollen grains per flower than insect-pollinated plants do.
Reason (R): Wind-pollinated grasses have a long feathery stigma that helps trap pollen grains.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A grass flower releases 9,00,000 pollen grains and forms 300 seeds, so about ___ pollen grains are released for each seed formed.

Match the pollinating agent with the matching example or feature.
1. Wind
2. Water
3. Insects
4. Birds
a. Coral tree flowers visited by sunbirds
b. Vallisneria and Hydrilla, with currents carrying the pollen
c. Light, small pollen in large numbers with a long feathery stigma
d. Brightly coloured, scented, nectar-rich flowers with large sticky pollen

A flower has a thin long tube joining its tip to a swollen base that holds small bodies, each with an egg cell.
(a) Name the three parts of this female organ from the tip to the base.
(b) Which of these parts receives the pollen, and why is it often flat or sticky?
questions.a: (a) Stigma, style and ovary. (b) The stigma receives the pollen; being flat or sticky helps it catch and hold the pollen grains.
s: Part (a): stigma, style, ovary in that order
Part (b): stigma, flat or sticky so it can catch pollen

questions.q: True or False? A breeder who removes the stamens from a flower bud and covers it with a bag prevents that flower from pollinating itself. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. With no anthers there is no pollen of its own, and the bag keeps unwanted pollen out until the chosen pollen is applied.
s: Verdict: True
Reason or correction: With no anthers there is no pollen of its own, and the bag keeps unwanted pollen out until the chosen pollen is applied

questions.q:
A flower is bright orange and scented, makes nectar, and has large sticky pollen.
(a) Which kind of pollinator is it adapted to?
(b) Explain how the sticky pollen helps this kind of pollination.
questions.a: (a) Insects such as bees and butterflies. (b) Sticky or spiny pollen attaches to the insect's body and is carried to the sticky stigma of another flower.
s: Part (a): insects such as bees and butterflies
Part (b): pollen attaches to the insect's body and is carried to a sticky stigma

questions.q: Differentiate self-pollination from cross-pollination, and give a field situation for each.
questions.a: Self-pollination: pollen goes to a stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant, e.g. a pea flower pollinating itself. Cross-pollination: pollen goes from the anther of one plant to the stigma of another plant of the same type, e.g. bees carrying pollen between two sunflower plants.
s: Self-pollination: same flower or same plant, with a situation
Cross-pollination: a different plant of the same type, with a situation

questions.q: After a tomato flower is fertilised, (a) what does its ovary become, and (b) what do the ovules become and what has formed from the fused gametes inside them?
questions.a: (a) The ovary enlarges into a fruit. (b) The ovules become seeds, and the zygote has developed into an embryo.
s: Part (a): ovary becomes a fruit
Part (b): ovules become seeds containing the embryo from the zygote

questions.q: Neha says, 'In the pea experiment the bud with its stamens removed formed no fruit, so the stamen is the part that makes the fruit.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The stamen matters because its anther supplies pollen, and pollen transfer to the stigma is needed for fruit to form; but the fruit itself develops from the ovary after fertilisation, not from the stamen.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: pollen from the anther must reach the stigma
Wrong part: the fruit comes from the ovary, not from the stamen

questions.q: Show that a pea flower whose stamens were all removed in the bud stage and which is kept covered with muslin until the pods form cannot develop a fruit.
questions.a: With no stamens there is no anther and no pollen, and the muslin keeps outside pollen away, so no pollen reaches the stigma; without pollination there is no pollen tube or fertilisation, so no fruit forms.
s: No stamens means no anther and no pollen of its own
The muslin stops pollen from outside reaching the stigma
No pollination, so no pollen tube, fertilisation or fruit

questions.q: Explain, with a reason each, why a maize flower has a long feathery stigma and a sunflower flower has a sticky stigma.
questions.a: Maize is wind-pollinated, and a long feathery stigma traps the light, small pollen grains floating in the air. The sunflower is insect-pollinated, and a sticky stigma holds the large, sticky or spiny pollen brought on an insect's body.
s: Maize is wind-pollinated, so a feathery stigma traps airborne pollen
Sunflower is insect-pollinated, so a sticky stigma holds pollen from the insect
Each stigma matches the pollen and the agent that carries it

questions.q:
A wind-pollinated grass releases 8,00,000 pollen grains per flower and forms 160 seeds. An insect-pollinated herb releases 32,000 pollen grains per flower and forms 640 seeds.
(i) Find the pollen grains released for each seed in both plants.
(ii) How many times more pollen does the grass use for each seed?
(iii) How many seeds does each plant form for every 1000 pollen grains?
(iv) Which plant forms more seeds per flower?
(v) Explain why releasing very large numbers of pollen grains can still work for the grass.
questions.a: (i) 5000 for the grass and 50 for the herb (ii) 100 times (iii) 0.2 and 20 (iv) the herb, with 640 against 160 (v) Wind carries pollen without aiming at a stigma, so only a tiny share arrives, and a huge number makes up for it.
s: 5000 and 50 pollen grains per seed
0.2 and 20 seeds per 1000 grains
The herb forms more seeds per flower
Wind pollination is not targeted, so large numbers make up for the loss

questions.q:
A farmer wants to cross a tall, disease-resistant maize variety (P) with a short, high-yield variety (Q) and use the pollen of P on the flowers of Q.
(i) What must she do to the Q flowers before they mature, and why?
(ii) What must she do next to keep unwanted pollen away?
(iii) How is pollen of P then used?
(iv) Name this method of plant breeding.
(v) Name one other plant-breeding method from the chapter and say how it works.
questions.a: (i) Remove the stamens, so the flower cannot pollinate itself. (ii) Cover it with a bag. (iii) Transfer the pollen of P by hand to the stigma of Q. (iv) Artificial hybridisation. (v) Selective breeding (choose plants with desired characters for reproduction) or genetic engineering (insert genetic material for the desired character).
s: Remove the stamens to prevent self-pollination
Cover the flower with a bag
Transfer the chosen pollen by hand to the stigma
Artificial hybridisation named
A second method named with how it works

questions.q:
Lakshmi grows sunflower on two plots of 4000 flower heads each. Plot A has 10 bee boxes placed at the edge; plot B has none. At harvest, the average seeds per head are 850 on plot A and 340 on plot B. Every 10,000 seeds earn her Rs 90, and each bee box costs Rs 1500 for the season.
(a) Name two features of a sunflower that help bees do this work.
(b) How many seeds does each plot give in all?
(c) Find the extra income from plot A and the extra income after paying for the boxes.
(d) Should she use bee boxes next year? Give one point from the money and one from the flowers' pollination.
questions.a: (a) Brightly coloured, fragrant, nectar-producing flowers with large sticky or spiny pollen and a sticky stigma. (b) 34,00,000 and 13,60,000. (c) Rs 18,360 more, and Rs 3,360 after paying Rs 15,000. (d) Yes, a modest gain that also makes sure cross-pollination happens; she could check against a year with fewer boxes since the margin is thin.
s: Two correct insect-pollination features
Rs 18,360 extra, Rs 3,360 after Rs 15,000 of boxes
A reasoned decision with a money point and a pollination point

questions.q:
A school garden group wrapped 20 flowers of a pea plant in each of five treatments and counted the fruits formed. T1: flower bud, wrapped: 18 fruits. T2: flower bud with stamens removed, wrapped: 0 fruits. T3: open flower with stamens removed, wrapped: 17 fruits. T4: open flower, wrapped: 19 fruits. T5: open flower, not wrapped: 20 fruits.
(a) Find the percentage of flowers forming fruit in each treatment.
(b) What does T2 show about pollen and fruit?
(c) T3 also had its stamens removed, yet formed fruit. Suggest a reason.
(d) A breeder wants controlled crosses. Which treatment is the best starting model and what must be added to it?
questions.a: (a) 90, 0, 85, 95 and 100 percent. (b) Fruit needs pollen transferred from the anther to the stigma; with the stamens removed early, none reached it. (c) Pollen had probably reached the stigma before the stamens were removed. (d) T2, since it blocks self-pollination, and then the chosen pollen must be placed on the stigma by hand.
s: 90, 0, 85, 95 and 100 percent
Without pollen transfer there is no fruit
Pollen may have been transferred before the stamens were removed
T2 as the model, with manual transfer of the chosen pollen

questions.q: In a monsoon pond, a female frog releases thousands of eggs into the water and a male frog releases sperm over them. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Fertilisation is external, and many of the eggs will be destroyed by currents or eaten
o: Fertilisation is external, and many of the eggs will be destroyed by currents or eaten
Fertilisation is internal, and the eggs are protected inside the female's body
Fertilisation is external, and nearly all the eggs will survive because water protects them
Fertilisation is internal, and the female will feed the young with milk after hatching

questions.q: A goat gives birth to one or two kids, while a carp lays hundreds of eggs. Which reason best explains why the goat can manage with so few young ones?
questions.a: Fertilisation is inside her body, so the embryo is protected and the chances of survival are generally higher
o: Fertilisation is inside her body, so the embryo is protected and the chances of survival are generally higher
Her eggs are released into water, which gives them more food than eggs in the open air
Her young ones are fertilised by many sperm, so each kid survives on its own after birth
Her eggs have no need for protection because the sperm are released over them in the water

questions.q: A school quiz asks which list contains only animals that show internal fertilisation. Which list should the students pick?
questions.a: Lizard, crow and goat
o: Lizard, crow and goat
Frog, crow and goat
Lizard, carp and goat
Hilsa fish, lizard and crow

questions.q: A hypothetical fish lays 1500 eggs and 6 reach adulthood. A hypothetical bird pair lays 4 eggs and 3 chicks grow up. What does a comparison of the survival rates show?
questions.a: The fish loses most eggs, with 0.4 percent surviving, while the bird saves most of its young, with 75 percent surviving
o: The fish loses most eggs, with 0.4 percent surviving, while the bird saves most of its young, with 75 percent surviving
The fish is the better parent, since 6 adults are produced from 1500 eggs against only 3 from the bird
Both survive at about the same rate because each species leaves a few adults behind
The bird loses more of its young, since it lays fewer than the fish does in each attempt

questions.q:
Statement 1: In animals with internal fertilisation, the chances of survival of the young ones are generally higher.
Statement 2: In every animal species the young ones are ready to find their own food as soon as they are born.
Statement 3: Fish and frogs bring their gametes together inside the body of the female.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Fish and frogs produce only a handful of eggs at a time.
Reason (R): Many of the eggs laid in water are destroyed by currents or eaten by other animals.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: A frog lays 20,000 eggs, and 40 of the young survive to adulthood. The percentage that survive is ___.

Match the animal with what it does or shows.
1. Frog
2. Crow
3. Butterfly
4. Goat
a. Lays eggs after fertilisation inside the female's body
b. Life cycle of egg, larva, pupa and adult
c. Female releases eggs into water and male releases sperm over them
d. Feeds its young with breast milk after birth

Fish lay hundreds to thousands of eggs at a time.
(a) Name the type of fertilisation in fish.
(b) Use your answer to explain why laying so many eggs makes sense for them.
questions.a: (a) External fertilisation. (b) The eggs are unprotected in the water and many are destroyed by currents or eaten, so laying very many makes it likelier that some young survive.
s: Part (a): external fertilisation
Part (b): unprotected eggs are lost in large numbers, so a high number improves survival chances

questions.q: True or False? Animals with internal fertilisation never need to look after their young ones once they are born. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. In many species the young ones need an extended period of care after birth, and mammals feed their young with breast milk.
s: Verdict: False
Reason or correction: In many species the young ones need an extended period of care after birth, and mammals feed their young with breast milk

questions.q:
Some young animals are ready to find their own food at birth, while others need long care.
(a) What does this difference broadly depend on?
(b) Name the way mammals typically feed their young after birth.
questions.a: (a) How long the embryo develops inside the egg or the mother's body. (b) Breast milk.
s: Part (a): the length of the embryo's development inside the egg or the mother's body
Part (b): mammals feed the young with breast milk

questions.q: State two dangers faced by eggs in external fertilisation and explain how internal fertilisation reduces them.
questions.a: Eggs may be destroyed by water currents or eaten by other animals. In internal fertilisation the fertilised egg or embryo stays inside the female's body and is better protected.
s: Two dangers: destroyed by currents, eaten by other animals
Internal fertilisation protects the fertilised egg or embryo, raising survival

questions.q:
A frog lays 30,000 eggs in a pond and only 0.1 percent of the young survive.
(a) How many young survive?
(b) Why does such a species still continue to exist?
questions.a: (a) 30 young. (b) The very large number of eggs makes up for the heavy losses, so some survive to grow up and reproduce.
s: Part (b): large numbers of eggs offset the heavy losses so that some survive

questions.q: Sunil says, 'Because a frog lays thousands of eggs at a time, more of its young survive than those of an animal with internal fertilisation.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. A frog lays a very large number of eggs, but the survival of its young is low, because the eggs are destroyed or eaten; with internal fertilisation the survival of young is generally higher.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
A large number of eggs does not mean more survivors, since survival is low
Internal fertilisation protects the embryo, so survival is generally higher

questions.q: Describe an animal, real or imagined, that follows internal fertilisation, gives birth to only a few young ones, and cares for them after birth. State what each choice does for the survival of the young.
questions.a: E.g. a cow: fertilisation inside her body protects the embryo; she has one calf at a time; she feeds the calf with her milk, so its survival is more likely.
s: Internal fertilisation named with protection of the embryo
Few young produced at a time
Post-birth care such as milk, linked to survival

questions.q: A frog and a goat have very different ways of making sure that the species continues. Describe each in one line and say what they have in common.
questions.a: The frog uses external fertilisation and lays very many eggs, accepting heavy losses. The goat uses internal fertilisation, has few young, protects the embryo and feeds the young with milk. Both ensure that gametes meet and that some young survive to reproduce.
s: Frog: external fertilisation with a very large number of eggs
Goat: internal fertilisation, few young, protection and milk
Common aim: gametes meet and young survive long enough to reproduce

questions.q:
A female frog lays 25,000 eggs and 0.4 percent of them become adults. A hypothetical bird pair lays 4 eggs and raises 3 chicks.
(i) How many frog eggs become adults?
(ii) What percentage of the bird's eggs give chicks that grow up?
(iii) How many frog eggs are laid for each adult that survives?
(iv) How many bird eggs are laid for each chick that survives (to 2 decimal places)?
(v) Explain the trade-off that the two species show.
questions.a: (i) 100 (ii) 75 percent (iii) 250 (iv) 1.33 (v) The frog trades heavy losses for huge numbers, while the bird protects a few eggs and gets a high survival.
s: 3 / 4 x 100 = 75 percent
The frog relies on numbers; the bird relies on protection and care

questions.q: Compare external fertilisation and internal fertilisation under these heads: (i) where the gametes meet, (ii) two animal examples of each, (iii) the number of eggs, (iv) protection of the egg or embryo, (v) the chances of survival of the young ones.
questions.a: (i) Outside the body in water, against inside the female's body. (ii) Frog and fish; reptiles, birds and mammals such as lizard and crow. (iii) Many against fewer. (iv) Little protection, against better protection. (v) Low against generally higher.
s: Place of fertilisation
Examples of each type
Number of eggs
Protection of egg or embryo
Survival of young

questions.q:
A fish hatchery in Andhra Pradesh keeps 8 breeding females, each laying 1200 eggs a cycle. In the open pond only 3 percent of the young survive; in the hatchery's protected tanks 55 percent survive. Each surviving fish sells for Rs 12, and running the hatchery tanks costs Rs 30,000 a cycle.
(a) Name the type of fertilisation in fish and give the main danger to the eggs in the pond.
(b) How many fish survive in the pond and in the hatchery?
(c) Find the money from the fish in each case and the hatchery's gain after its cost.
(d) Recommend a choice and name the feature of animals with internal fertilisation that the hatchery copies.
questions.a: (a) External fertilisation; the eggs are destroyed by currents or eaten. (b) 288 and 5280. (c) Rs 3,456 and Rs 63,360, so the hatchery gains Rs 33,360 after cost against Rs 3,456 in the pond. (d) Use the hatchery, which copies the protection of the egg or embryo that raises survival.
s: External fertilisation; danger of destruction or being eaten
9600 eggs give 288 and 5280 survivors
Rs 3,456 and Rs 63,360, with Rs 33,360 after the Rs 30,000 cost
Hatchery recommended, linked to protection of eggs as in internal fertilisation

questions.q:
A village livestock project compares a fish pond with a goat shed. Each fish female lays 1000 eggs and 1 percent of the young survive. Each nanny goat has 2 kids and 90 percent survive, but the kids need milk for the first weeks and the goats need steady care after birth. The project has few helpers and wants to increase the animals quickly.
(a) Name the type of fertilisation in each animal.
(b) Find the number of survivors per female in each case.
(c) Explain why the goat's young need the care described.
(d) The project can keep either 10 fish females or 10 nanny goats. Decide which gives more animals and name one other factor to weigh.
questions.a: (a) Fish: external; goat: internal. (b) 10 fish and 1.8 kids. (c) A mammal's young typically feed on breast milk after birth and may need extended care depending on how developed they are. (d) 10 fish females give 100 against 18 kids, so the fish pond gives more animals; the care and time needed by the goats is another factor, since the helpers are few.
s: External for fish, internal for goat
Mammals feed the young with milk and give care after birth
100 against 18 kids, with a stated second factor such as care effort

questions.q: A doctor explains to a class that the testes lie in a pouch of skin outside the main body cavity. What is the reason given in the chapter?
questions.a: It keeps the testes slightly cooler than the body, as sperm formation needs
o: It keeps the testes slightly cooler than the body, as sperm formation needs
It keeps the testes warmer than the rest of the body, which speeds up the sperm
It stores the urine that later mixes with the sperm in the urethra before they leave
It adds the fluids that nourish the sperm and help them to remain active and move

questions.q: Which route correctly shows how a sperm leaves the body, and which glands add fluid on the way?
questions.a: Testis, vas deferens, urethra; the seminal vesicles and prostate add fluids
o: Testis, vas deferens, urethra; the seminal vesicles and prostate add fluids
Testis, urethra, vas deferens; the scrotum and the ovary add fluids to carry the sperm
Testis, scrotum, urethra; the oviduct and the uterus add fluids to help the sperm swim
Testis, vas deferens, vagina; the seminal vesicles and the cervix add fluids to feed the sperm

questions.q: A sperm succeeds in fusing with an egg released this month. Where does the fusion take place, and what happens next?
questions.a: In the oviduct; the zygote divides by mitosis on its way to implant in the uterus
o: In the oviduct; the zygote divides by mitosis on its way to implant in the uterus
In the uterus; the zygote then travels back to the oviduct and implants in the ovary lining
In the vagina; the zygote then divides by meiosis and moves up to the uterus without a lining
In the ovary; the zygote then divides by meiosis and the uterine lining is shed at once

questions.q: In a family with three daughters, a relative blames the mother for not having a son. Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The mother always gives X; the baby's sex depends on whether the father's sperm carried X or Y
o: The mother always gives X; the baby's sex depends on whether the father's sperm carried X or Y
The mother decides, because her eggs are of two kinds, one carrying X and the other carrying Y chromosomes
The father always gives a Y chromosome, so the sex of the baby depends on the mother's egg alone
Neither parent decides, because the sex of the baby depends on which of the two parents is older

questions.q:
Statement 1: The ovaries produce eggs and also release hormones.
Statement 2: From puberty, usually one mature egg is released from an ovary every month.
Statement 3: In IVF, an egg and a sperm are combined outside the female body, usually in a laboratory dish.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements
o: All three statements
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): If an egg is not fertilised, the thickened lining of the uterus is shed along with some blood.
Reason (R): The lining that thickened and became rich in blood vessels to nourish a zygote is no longer needed.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Neelam's period began on 18 February 2026 and her cycle is 26 days long. Her next period is expected on ___ (give the date).
questions.a: 16 March

questions.q:
Match the organ with its role or feature.
1. Scrotum
2. Oviduct
3. Cervix
4. Seminal vesicle
a. Narrow passage through which the uterus opens into the vagina
b. Adds fluid that nourishes the sperm
c. Keeps the testes slightly cooler than body temperature
d. Connects each ovary to the uterus

Human body cells have 46 chromosomes.
(a) How many chromosomes does a sperm and an egg have?
(b) How many does the zygote have, and why does this matter?
questions.a: (a) 23 in each. (b) 46, so the zygote has the same number as the parents' body cells and the number does not double.
s: Part (a): 23 in a sperm and 23 in an egg
Part (b): 46 in the zygote, keeping the chromosome number the same as in the parents

questions.q: True or False? When an egg is not fertilised, the thickened lining of the uterus is shed through the vagina because it is no longer needed. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The lining became thick and rich in blood vessels to nourish a zygote, and with no zygote it leaves with some blood as menstruation.
s: Verdict: True
Reason or correction: The lining became thick and rich in blood vessels to nourish a zygote, and with no zygote it leaves with some blood as menstruation

questions.q:
Table 11.5 compares sperm and egg.
(a) State how the two differ in the number produced and in motility.
(b) Which part of a sperm helps it swim towards the egg, and which part carries its genetic material?
questions.a: (a) Sperm are produced in millions and are actively motile; eggs are few and non-motile. (b) The tail helps it swim; the head carries the genetic material.
s: Part (a): millions and motile for sperm, few and non-motile for egg
Part (b): tail for swimming, head for genetic material

questions.q: A newspaper calls a baby born by IVF a 'test tube baby'. (a) Where do the egg and sperm actually combine in IVF? (b) What is done with the fertilised egg afterwards?
questions.a: (a) Outside the female body, usually in a laboratory culture dish and not in a test tube. (b) It is implanted in the uterus to begin a possible pregnancy.
s: Part (a): outside the body, usually in a laboratory dish
Part (b): the fertilised egg is implanted in the uterus

questions.q:
In a typical 28-day menstrual cycle, with day 1 as the first day of menstruation:
(a) On which day does ovulation occur?
(b) What happens to the lining of the uterus between days 15 and 28 if no fertilisation occurs?
questions.a: (a) Day 14. (b) The lining becomes thicker and rich with blood vessels, and at about day 28 it starts breaking down.
s: Part (a): day 14
Part (b): the lining thickens, then starts breaking down around day 28

questions.q: Deepa says, 'A zygote has 46 chromosomes because the sperm gives 23 and the egg gives 23, and the fusion usually happens in the oviduct.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Yes. Both gametes are formed by meiosis and carry 23 chromosomes, so 23 + 23 = 46, and the sperm usually meets the egg in the oviduct.
s: Verdict: the claim is correct
23 + 23 = 46 from the two gametes
Fusion usually takes place in the oviduct

questions.q: Show that the mother cannot be the parent who decides whether a baby will be a boy or a girl.
questions.a: Every egg carries an X chromosome, so the mother always contributes an X. The baby is a girl (XX) if the sperm carries X and a boy (XY) if it carries Y, so the father's sperm decides.
s: The mother always contributes an X chromosome
The father contributes either X (girl) or Y (boy)
So the difference comes only from the father's sperm

questions.q: Describe what happens to the lining of the uterus on days 1 to 5, days 6 to 14 and days 15 to 28 of a typical 28-day cycle, and say what the ovary does on day 14.
questions.a: Days 1 to 5: the lining is shed (menstruation). Days 6 to 14: the lining gradually rebuilds while an egg matures. Day 14: the ovary releases a mature egg. Days 15 to 28: the lining becomes thicker and rich with blood vessels.
s: Days 1 to 5: shedding
Days 6 to 14: lining rebuilds as the egg matures
Day 14 ovulation and days 15 to 28 thickening

questions.q:
A girl's 28-day cycle begins on 4 June (day 1).
(i) On which date does ovulation occur (day 14)?
(ii) On which date does the lining begin to break down (about day 28)?
(iii) When does her next period begin?
(iv) How many whole cycles of 28 days fit in a year of 365 days?
(v) Explain why the lining of the uterus thickens during each cycle.
questions.a: (i) 17 June (ii) 1 July (iii) 2 July (iv) 13 (v) The lining thickens to prepare for receiving a zygote that might form after ovulation.
s: Day 14 is 17 June
Day 28 is 1 July
The next period starts on day 29, 2 July
365 / 28 gives 13 whole cycles
The lining prepares to receive and nourish a zygote

questions.q: Trace the events from the release of an egg to the beginning of a pregnancy, in order: (i) where the egg goes after ovulation, (ii) how the sperm reach it, (iii) what forms when one sperm fuses with it, (iv) what the zygote does while travelling, (v) what marks the beginning of pregnancy.
questions.a: (i) The egg travels from the ovary to the oviduct. (ii) Millions of sperm enter through the vagina and swim through the tract to the oviduct. (iii) A zygote forms. (iv) It divides by mitosis on the way to the uterus. (v) Implantation in the thickened lining.
s: The egg moves from the ovary to the oviduct
Sperm enter through the vagina and swim to the oviduct
Fusion of one sperm and the egg forms a zygote
Mitotic divisions while it travels to the uterus
Implantation in the thickened lining marks the start of pregnancy

questions.q:
A school wants to stock its girls' washroom. Guidelines say that a pad should be changed every 4 to 6 hours, and menstruation usually lasts up to 5 days for most girls in this school. Assume a girl is awake for 16 hours a day. A disposable pad costs Rs 6; a set of 6 reusable pads costs Rs 300, lasts 24 cycles, and must be washed and dried completely before use.
(a) State two other hygiene practices from the chapter besides changing the pad regularly.
(b) Find the least and the greatest number of pads one girl needs in a 5-day period.
(c) Compare the cost per girl over 24 cycles for the greatest number of disposable pads and for one reusable set.
(d) Which should the school choose? Give one point on cost and one on a practical or hygiene need.
questions.a: (a) E.g. wash hands with soap before and after changing, and wrap and bin used pads without flushing. (b) 15 and 20. (c) Rs 2,880 for disposable pads against Rs 300 for a reusable set. (d) Reusable pads are cheaper, but they need clean water, privacy and complete drying; the school could offer both, or give disposable pads for the school day.
s: Two valid hygiene practices from the chapter
3 pads x 5 = 15 and 4 x 5 = 20
20 x 6 x 24 = Rs 2,880 against Rs 300
A reasoned choice with a cost point and a practical or hygiene point

questions.q:
A newspaper headline reads, 'Baby grown in a test tube for nine months'. A student wants to correct the report using her textbook. A baby born through IVF began as an egg and a sperm combined outside the mother's body.
(a) Where do the egg and sperm combine in IVF, and how many chromosomes does each gamete carry?
(b) How many chromosomes does the fertilised egg carry?
(c) What is done with the fertilised egg after fertilisation, and which step of ordinary reproduction does it then follow?
(d) Judge the headline: what part is right, what part is wrong, and how would you correct it?
questions.a: (a) Outside the female body, usually in a laboratory dish; 23 each. (b) 46. (c) It is implanted in the uterus, where implantation marks the beginning of pregnancy. (d) Right: fertilisation occurred outside the body. Wrong: the baby does not grow for nine months in a test tube or dish; it develops in the uterus during pregnancy. Corrected: fertilisation was in a dish and the pregnancy was in the uterus.
s: Outside the body, in a dish; 23 chromosomes in each gamete
Implanted in the uterus, then pregnancy proceeds as usual
A balanced judgement of what is right and wrong, with a corrected headline

questions.q: Ritu is ten weeks into her pregnancy. What is the developing baby called, and in which trimester is she?
questions.a: A foetus, in the first trimester
o: A foetus, in the first trimester
An embryo, in the second trimester
A foetus, in the third trimester
An embryo, in the first trimester

questions.q: A neighbour offers a pregnant woman a tablet bought at a shop for a cold, saying it is harmless. What does the chapter's advice suggest she should do?
questions.a: Take none unless a doctor advises it, as harmful substances can affect the baby
o: Take none unless a doctor advises it, as harmful substances can affect the baby
Take it, because a short course of any tablet cannot affect the growth of the baby at all
Take it only if she also stops her regular check-ups and rests completely in bed
Take it after the first trimester, when medicines are no longer any concern to the baby

questions.q: A couple wants a method that prevents pregnancy and also lowers the chance of passing on infections such as gonorrhoea or HIV. Which method named in the chapter fits?
questions.a: A condom, which acts as a barrier and prevents transmission
o: A condom, which acts as a barrier and prevents transmission
Oral pills, which change the release of eggs through hormones
A Copper-T, placed in the uterus to avoid pregnancy
Blocking the fallopian tubes, so that the sperm and egg cannot meet

questions.q: Rohan, aged 15, says, 'My voice has changed and I am growing fast, so I am ready for adult responsibilities.' Which reply fits the chapter best?
questions.a: Body changes come gradually, but emotional maturity, such as handling feelings, takes longer
o: Body changes come gradually, but emotional maturity, such as handling feelings, takes longer
He is right, because sexual maturity brings emotional maturity along with it at the same speed
He is right, since a body that is able to reproduce can already make all adult decisions
He is wrong, because no change in the body happens before adulthood begins at eighteen

questions.q:
Statement 1: Condoms prevent pregnancy but cannot reduce the transmission of sexually transmitted infections.
Statement 2: Sexual maturity during adolescence brings emotional maturity along with it at the same time.
Statement 3: Surgical methods of preventing pregnancy include blocking the vas deferens in males or the fallopian tubes in females.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 3 only
o: Statement 3 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Breastfeeding is essential for a newborn baby.
Reason (R): Newborns must be kept warm, vaccinated on time and handled gently.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A couple wants one method that prevents both pregnancy and the transmission of STIs. The method named in the chapter is the ___.
questions.a: condom

questions.q:
Match the contraceptive with how it works or its feature.
1. Copper-T
2. Oral pill
3. Surgical method
4. Condom
a. Placed in the uterus and may sometimes irritate it
b. Blocks the vas deferens or the fallopian tubes
c. A barrier that stops sperm reaching the egg and helps prevent STIs
d. Medicine that changes the release of eggs by altering hormones

Meera has been pregnant for 7 months.
(a) In which trimester is she?
(b) What is the baby doing in this trimester?
questions.a: (a) The third trimester. (b) The baby grows rapidly and gets ready for life outside the womb.
s: Part (a): third trimester, as months 7 to 9
Part (b): rapid growth and preparing for life outside the womb

questions.q: True or False? Post-partum depression is a recognised condition that can be treated, so a mother who feels low or overwhelmed after delivery should be encouraged to talk to a healthcare worker. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.

questions.q: Differentiate sexual maturity from emotional maturity in adolescence, with one example of each.
questions.a: Sexual maturity is the body becoming capable of reproduction, which happens gradually (sperm production in boys, menstrual cycles in girls). Emotional maturity is handling feelings, communicating clearly and making thoughtful decisions, and it takes longer.
s: Sexual maturity: the body is capable of reproduction, with an example
Emotional maturity: handling feelings, clear communication, thoughtful decisions, which takes longer

questions.q: State one possible drawback each of the oral pill and of the Copper-T, and say which of the two works by altering hormones.
questions.a: Oral pills may have side effects; a Copper-T may sometimes irritate the uterus. The oral pill works by altering hormones.
s: Pill: possible side effects; Copper-T: may irritate the uterus
The oral pill is the one that alters hormones to change the release of eggs

questions.q: (a) Give two things a pregnant woman should do or avoid for her own health and the baby's. (b) Give two things a newborn needs.
questions.a: (a) E.g. eat a balanced diet and attend regular check-ups; avoid smoking, alcohol and medicines without medical advice. (b) Breastfeeding, warmth, timely vaccination and gentle handling (any two).
s: Part (a): two valid points on a mother's care
Part (b): two valid needs of a newborn

questions.q: Kiran says, 'Blocking the fallopian tubes in women and the vas deferens in men prevents unwanted pregnancy, and it also prevents sexually transmitted infections.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. These surgical methods stop the sperm and egg from meeting, so they prevent pregnancy; but the chapter names condoms, not surgical methods, as preventing the transmission of STIs.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: sperm and egg cannot meet, so pregnancy is prevented
Wrong part: the chapter gives condoms as the method that prevents transmission of STIs

questions.q: Write a short situation in which a Class 9 student explains to a friend why a body that has grown mature is not the same as being ready for adult responsibilities. Include two features of emotional maturity.
questions.a: E.g. Asha tells her friend that although her body has grown and changed, being ready means handling feelings, communicating clearly and making thoughtful choices, which come later than the physical changes.
s: A realistic situation
Physical maturity is distinguished from emotional maturity
Two features: handling feelings, clear communication, thoughtful decisions

questions.q: Explain, in a chain of cause and effect, why prenatal sex determination is strictly prohibited by law in India.
questions.a: A preference for a particular gender can lead to self-selective abortion; this can cause a marked imbalance in the societal sex ratio; the law protects the sex ratio for a healthy, forward-looking society.
s: Preference for one gender can lead to self-selective abortion
This causes a marked imbalance in the sex ratio
The law protects the sex ratio for a healthy society

questions.q:
Rani's pregnancy lasts about nine months in three trimesters of equal length. The embryo is called a foetus from about the ninth week.
(i) How many months does each trimester last?
(ii) About how many months old is the pregnancy at the ninth week (take 52 weeks = 12 months, to one decimal place)?
(iii) Rani feels the baby move in her fifth month. Which trimester is this?
(iv) In which trimester does the baby grow rapidly, ready for life outside?
(v) Describe how the baby is pushed out at childbirth, and what may be done if a normal birth is not safe.
questions.a: (i) 3 months (ii) about 2.1 months (iii) second (iv) third (v) Strong contractions of the uterine muscles push the foetus through the birth canal; doctors may use medical or surgical procedures to deliver the baby safely.
s: 9 / 3 = 3 months per trimester
9 / (52/12) = about 2.1 months
Month 5 is in the second trimester
Rapid growth and readiness for birth is in the third trimester
Contractions push the foetus out; medical or surgical help if unsafe

questions.q: Prepare a care plan, with a reason for each line, for a new mother and her baby: (i) the baby's feeding, (ii) two other needs of the newborn, (iii) the mother's diet and rest, (iv) two things she should avoid, (v) what to do if she feels low or overwhelmed after delivery.
questions.a: (i) Breastfeeding, since milk gives complete nutrition and protects against many diseases. (ii) Keep the baby warm and vaccinated on time, with gentle handling. (iii) Nutritious food and adequate rest. (iv) Smoking, alcohol, medicines without medical advice. (v) Talk to a healthcare worker, since post-partum depression is a recognised, treatable condition.
s: Breastfeeding with its reason
Two newborn needs from warmth, vaccination, gentle handling
Nutritious food and adequate rest
Two harmful habits or medicines to avoid
Talk to a healthcare worker about post-partum depression

questions.q:
In a town, the hospital records of one year show 2000 births: 1070 boys and 930 girls. The health officer links the gap to a preference for boys that can lead to a practice the chapter calls a serious concern.
(a) Name the practice and the law that is meant to stop it.
(b) Find the number of girls born per 1000 boys, to the nearest whole number.
(c) By how many do the boys outnumber the girls?
(d) The officer can run one of two programmes: strict inspection of clinics, or awareness sessions in schools and villages. Give one point for each and recommend one.
questions.a: (a) Self-selective abortion based on gender; prenatal sex determination is prohibited by law. (b) 869. (c) 140. (d) Inspection enforces the law quickly but cannot change the preference; awareness changes attitudes over time but is slower; a combination with the first as the immediate step is sensible.
s: Self-selective abortion and the legal prohibition of prenatal sex determination
A point for each programme and a reasoned recommendation

questions.q:
Three weeks after delivering a baby, Sunita feels anxious, very tired and low, and sometimes cries without a reason. Her mother-in-law says it is only laziness. Because Sunita is tired, the family plans to stop breastfeeding and give the baby diluted cow's milk from next week so that she can rest.
(a) Name Sunita's condition and say whether it can be treated.
(b) Whom should the family encourage her to talk to?
(c) What does the chapter say a mother's milk gives to the baby?
(d) Judge the family's two decisions, and suggest a plan that gives Sunita rest and protects the baby.
questions.a: (a) Post-partum depression; it is a recognised condition that can be treated. (b) A healthcare worker such as a doctor or nurse. (c) Complete nutrition and protection from many diseases. (d) Calling it laziness is wrong because the condition is recognised and treatable; stopping breastfeeding gives up the milk's complete nutrition and protection. A better plan: keep breastfeeding, share household work so she can rest, and get help from a healthcare worker.
s: Post-partum depression, which is treatable
A healthcare worker such as a doctor, nurse or similar
Complete nutrition and protection from many diseases
Both decisions judged and a plan that keeps breastfeeding and arranges rest and help
